name: Lateral raise
angleNote: 0° = arm by your side, 90° = arm horizontal at shoulder height. Front view: x points out to the side.

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end (forearm includes the hand). Approximate textbook anthropometry.

segments.note: Shoulder→elbow and elbow→grip centre in metres, typical adult. The arm is modelled straight; a soft elbow shortens the lever slightly.

strengthCurve.label: Shoulder abductor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative isometric shoulder-abduction torque vs angle, assumed to fall off as the arm rises. Approximate shape.
strengthCurve.source: TODO: verify against published isometric/isokinetic shoulder-abduction torque–angle data

muscles.name: Lateral deltoid
muscles.note: Main abductor once the arm is away from the side; its moment arm grows as the arm rises. wger has no separate map for the lateral head.

muscles.name: Supraspinatus
muscles.note: Helps start the raise and keeps the head of the humerus centred in the socket; relatively more important early in the range.

muscles.name: Anterior deltoid
muscles.note: Assists abduction, and takes over more if the arm drifts forward of the body.

muscles.name: Upper trapezius
muscles.note: Rotates the shoulder blade upwards as the arm rises. Shown on the back body map.

phases.name: Start
phases.text: Arm by your side. A dumbbell's line of action passes close to the shoulder, so there's little torque here. A cable from the opposite side already pulls the arm across the body.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: The free-weight moment arm grows with the sine of the angle. The deltoid's leverage improves too, and the shoulder blade starts to rotate upwards.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Arm near horizontal. With a dumbbell the moment arm is the full arm length just as abductor strength is falling off, so this is the sticking point.

variants.name: Standing dumbbell lateral raise
variants.notes: Gravity pulls straight down, so torque = m·g·L·sin(angle): zero with the arm by your side and maximum at shoulder height. The bottom of the range is almost unloaded.

variants.name: Cable lateral raise (low pulley, opposite side)
variants.notes: The cable comes from a low pulley on the other side of your body, so it pulls the arm across you even at the bottom. The torque curve is much flatter than with a dumbbell. In this flat front view the cable seems to pass through the body; in reality it runs just in front of or behind it.

variants.name: Lateral raise machine

camProfile.note: Effective radius in metres: joint torque per unit of stack weight, including any lever or pulley ratio. Illustrative shape, not measured from a specific machine.

variants.notes: A pad on the upper arm near the elbow pushes against the raise, and the cam sets the resistance at each angle. This illustrative cam loads the start far more than a dumbbell and stays fairly even. Machine stack weights don't compare directly with dumbbell weights: the same number of kg gives a different torque.
